comments.text: I recommand David Beazley's talk from a recent PyCon India on a similar subject : [VIDEO] Mostly live coded, it really is pretty amazing but also quite insightful.

I found this [1] quite interesting. It doesn't really answer any of the questions you asked, but I think it gives some interesting insights into WebAssembly, which might make it easier to put other things in context and also give a good low level understanding of it. It's the closing keynote talk at this year's PyCon India. From the description: > In this talk, I live-code a simple stack machine and turn it into an interpreter capable of running WebAssembly. I then use that to play a game written in Rust. [VIDEO]

comments.story: Ask HN: What piece of code/codebase blew your mind when you saw it?
comments.text: There was a youtube video a few years back that showed a guy livecoding...I think an ECMA interpreter, or maybe a WASM interpreter from scratch using some very easy to follow code. I can't remember what it was or the video, but it was gobsmacking. So instead here's another story. I once worked with an old Perl greybeard, he had written some kind of code that could parse an almost impossible large set of string formats that a large collection of automated systems produced except they all had some sort of non-standard/non-guaranteed formatting or semantics. Little bits and pieces (some semi-atomic bits) of them were semi-reliable, but the aggregate strings were just a huge mess, things came in all kinds of orders, had unreliable separators (if any) some things came in backwards, some forwards, and so on. You might imagine them to be things like IP addresses that sometimes had system names…
